quotes.text: Answer true betrayal once, then cast the stones again.
"You could keep them all," he whispered. "Grandfather is gone. Who would know?"
"The river knows. The stranger knows. And I would know.
"The mist steals, not your friend."
"Why throw everything, grandfather? What if she keeps it all?"
That night the villages carved a tenth mark on the willow
"Footprints like these are a promise," he said, and he threw all five.
*Judge the hand, not the mist. Return more than half. Keep the river flowing.*

note: River of Three Waters; Anwe's law: give fully, return a little more, forgive the fog, answer true betrayal once; later just judge the hand.

quotes.text: Some potters whispered that it was time to hoard.
Who would know, in such mist?
*The mist lies, but the pattern does not.*
Her apprentice asked why she never tested the strangers.
"What if I keep one lump back, only to be safe?"
So the potters carved the seventh line above the kiln:
The shelf held no names, only patterns: which hands had given fully, which had returned fairly.
The shelf no longer recorded debts. It recorded a habit.
*When you hold the clay, give it whole to open hands. The kiln multiplies only what you release.*

note: Tessor kiln and shard shelf; carved lines each winter; give fully, return beyond the risk, forgive the fog; whispers to hoard rejected.

quotes.text: His young guide whispered, "The sand swallowed part of the gift. Return only half."
The wise ones never blamed the giver for the wind.
"Why should the giver end richer?" the apprentice asked.
"He carried the risk," Torvald answered. "When bold hands prosper, every forge burns hotter."
In the island realm of Veloria, eight fishers shared the waters of the Tide Mother.
*Give whole. Return more than half. Read the bark, not the dew.*
But the Fire Father kept a great ledger of bronze, and every gift and every return was engraved there for all to read.

note: New realm each round on one skeleton: eight X share a Mother's law, a public record, give whole, return more than half.

quotes.text: If it comes thin always, then guard your grain.
"Then his knots will show it, and we will cast more carefully toward that hand.
The mist whispered, "Keep it. The stranger cannot see through fog. Who will ever know?"
"The willow would know, and so would I.
One thin basket is fog. Many thin baskets are a closed hand.
"Why do you never keep a loaf behind? Some of your returns came back thinner than you hoped."
The one who dares first must walk home richer than he came, or no one will dare again.
Return more than half, because the giver took the risk.
let the stories you tell match the bread you send
Wren tied her fifth knot
Nell showed him a knotted cord. Each knot marked a crossing
Wren tied her fifth knot: trust the proven, guard against the proven false, and let the mist be only mist.

note: Willow of Nell and knotted cord; guard grain only against repeated thinness; mist-whisper to hoard rejected; numbered knots.

quotes.text: The next season, no one planted in his field, and his five seeds stayed five.
If a crooked walker ever comes, his road will warn me, and I will give with care.
Her brother whispered, "The mist says he held back. Keep more for yourself."
as it should be for the one who dared first
"The giver carries the danger," Anwe replied.
"Blame the mist before you blame your kin."
"Why trust one you have never met?" asked his grandson.
"I would blame myself," Anwe said, "and the ledgers would remember.
The keepers carved a ninth line
The herders no longer asked who stood on the far bank, only how that stranger had walked before.
When old partners meet again, let the first trust ripen into a deeper one.

note: Mosk who returned nothing is shunned (R1); later lines: read the road, give whole to straight walkers, give with care to crooked ones.

quotes.text: If that day comes, I will read it in the stones and pour more carefully for that hand.
The quick-tempered travelers took offense and stopped pouring, and the well grew silent.
A merchant leaned close. "The sand hides everything. Keep the extra, and no one will know."
"The sand hides one pour. It cannot hide a lifetime of them, not Ilen's and not mine.
"The wind lies more often than your neighbor does.
"The pourer carries the danger. The receiver carries the debt."
"Why not repay the desert for what it took?" Oru asked.
Travelers learned to judge each stranger by their own hand, not by another's wound.
"Because he opened his hands first," Sefa said.
Oru carved a seventh line
"I trusted a story written in deeds.
Trust the proven fully. Guard only against the proven false.

note: Well of Three Waters; Sefa reads carved deeds, guards only against proven false; cheated Kesh not presumed a cheat.

quotes.text: A young traveler whispered, "Keep more this time. The mist will hide you."
"The mist can hide a single crossing. It cannot hide a trail of footprints, not hers and not mine."
"The wind deceives, not our kin.
"Because he carried the risk," Lio said.
"Why should the sender walk home richer than you?" the young one asked.
That night the keepers carved a seventh verse
Faces stayed hidden, but deeds left footprints on the reeds
When the mist blurs your gift, answer with a wider hand.

note: Bridge of Asha; footprints as reputation; numbered verses; whispers to keep more or hold back rejected; no sanction.

quotes.text: Answer a great betrayal only once, then offer the seed again.
A fox-merchant slipped from the fog. "The mist hides so much. Who would know if you kept ten?"
"I would," said Vessa, "and the reeds would sing it by nightfall.
"The mist steals, not your friend.
The old Heron watched from the shallows. "Why give more than you must?"
Judge each spirit by its own hand, not by the storms it endured.
but the reeds knew his story
Keep your measure steady for strangers and friends alike.

note: Heron: answer great betrayal once, then offer seed again; later only steady measure; fox-merchant tempter rejected.

phrase: give boldly, return fairly, forgive the fog/mist
note: Also shared: Heron's 'The mist steals, not your friend' and 'answer betrayal once' (Agents 1, 8); names Tamsi, Oru, Tavi, Lio cross myths.
